questions.question: Why do idiomatic `get` traps call `Reflect.get(target, key, receiver)` rather than returning `target[key]`?
options: Reflect.get is faster than property access
Passing the receiver keeps getters' `this` pointing at the proxy, so reads inside getters still go through the proxy
Reflect.get automatically makes the property reactive
questions.explanation: With target[key], a getter runs with `this` set to the raw target and bypasses the proxy. Reflect.get with the receiver preserves the proxy as `this`.

questions.question: What happens in strict mode code if a proxy's `set` trap returns false?
options: The value is written to the target anyway
questions.explanation: A set trap must return true to signal success; a falsy return throws a TypeError in strict mode, which includes modules and classes.

questions.question: Which is an example of a Proxy invariant the engine enforces?
options: A get trap must always return a string
ownKeys must include every non-configurable own key of the target
A proxy must be strictly equal (===) to its target
Every proxy must define all 13 traps
questions.explanation: Invariants keep proxies consistent with the target: for example ownKeys cannot omit non-configurable keys, and get must report the real value of a non-configurable, non-writable property. Violations throw a TypeError.

questions.question: Why could Vue 3's Proxy-based reactivity detect newly added properties when Vue 2 could not?
options: Vue 2 did not support objects, only arrays
Vue 3 polls objects for changes on every animation frame
Vue 2's Object.defineProperty getters/setters only existed for properties defined upfront, while a Proxy set trap intercepts writes to any key
Vue 3 uses WeakMap instead of Map, which tracks new keys automatically
questions.explanation: defineProperty instruments specific existing keys, so additions and array index writes went unnoticed (hence Vue.set). A Proxy intercepts the operation itself, for any key.
